title: Tangent spaces, Lie algebras and rational actions
statement: *Tangent spaces and differentials.* Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Let X=Spec A and Y=Spec B be finite-type affine k-schemes, let x in X(k), and let phi:X\to Y be a k-morphism. The tangent space is T_xX := T_{X/k,x} as defined in [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space], using the dual-number ring [def-sc-dual-numbers]. For rational points, [lem-sc-rational-tangent-cotangent-duality] identifies T_xX canonically with Hom_k(m_x/m_x^2,k), and [lem-sc-rational-point-tangent-derivation-identification] identifies its vectors with k-derivations at x. The differential d phi_x is induced by the tangent-map construction of [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space] (equivalently, under the preceding identification, the dual of the cotangent map); differentials compose. *Lie algebra of a matrix group.* Let V be a finite-dimensional k-vector space and let G be a finite-type closed subgroup scheme of GL(V). For a commutative k-algebra R, G(R) consists of matrices satisfying the defining equations. Define Lie(G) := T_{G/k,1}, identified with {X in End_k(V) | 1+epsilon X in G(k[epsilon]/epsilon^2)} via X \mapsto 1+epsilon X (and T_1 GL(V)=End_k(V)), using [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space] and [def-sc-dual-numbers]. By [lem-wf-lie-algebra-derivation-bracket], Lie(G) is a subspace of End_k(V) closed under the commutator [X,Y]=XY-YX, hence a Lie algebra in the sense of [def-wf-lie-algebra] under this bracket. *Rational actions.* Let M be a finite-dimensional k-vector space. For a regular homomorphism r:G\to GL(M) as in [def-wf-algebraic-representations], its differential at 1 is the linear map dr:Lie(G)\to End_k(M) characterized by r(1+epsilon X)=1+epsilon dr(X) over k[epsilon]/epsilon^2; by [lem-wf-lie-algebra-derivation-bracket] it is a Lie representation of Lie(G) on M in the sense of [def-wf-lie-algebra], i.e. dr([X,Y])=dr(X)dr(Y)-dr(Y)dr(X). The adjoint action is Ad(g)X=gXg^{-1} for g in G(k); it preserves Lie(G), since g(1+epsilon X)g^{-1}=1+epsilon gXg^{-1} and conjugation by g preserves G. Its differential is ad(Y)X=[Y,X], since over k[epsilon]/epsilon^2 one has (1+epsilon Y)X(1+epsilon Y)^{-1}=X+epsilon(YX-XY). *Matrix group schemes and smoothness.* A finite-type matrix group scheme is a finite-type closed subgroup scheme of GL(V), possibly nonreduced, with multiplication and inversion restricting from GL(V). Regular local rings and regular schemes use [def-weil-regular-scheme], and smooth ring maps use [def-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map]. For a finite-type affine k-scheme over the perfect base field k, the regular-local-ring criterion and its equivalence with smoothness at a point are the content of [lem-weil-pbc-regular-local-cotangent-dimension], [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-over-field-regular-local], and [lem-weil-pbc-regular-local-separable-residue-smooth]. A smooth matrix group is smooth at every closed point.

external.place: (That this subspace is closed under the bracket, and that $dr$ below preserves brackets, is standard: compare Milne, *Algebraic Groups* (2017), Chapter 10.) *Rational actions.* A *rational representation* of $G$ is a regular homomorphism $r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(M)$, i.e. an algebraic-group module in the sense of [def-wf-algebraic-representations].

blueprint_update.statement:
*Tangent spaces and differentials.* Let $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ be a
finite-type affine $k$-scheme (for instance an affine variety, i.e.
$A$ finitely generated and reduced) and let $x\in X(k)$, with maximal
ideal $\mathfrak m_x\subseteq A$ of the functions vanishing at $x$. The
*tangent space* of $X$ at $x$ is

$$
T_xX=(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)^\vee
=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2,k).
$$

Equivalently, $T_xX$ is the set of $k$-algebra maps
$A\to k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$ reducing to evaluation at $x$
modulo $\varepsilon$: such a map is $f\mapsto f(x)+\varepsilon\,v(f)$
with $v$ a $k$-derivation at $x$, and $v\mapsto v|_{\mathfrak m_x}$
identifies these derivations with the linear forms on $\mathfrak m_x$
killing $\mathfrak m_x^2$. A regular map
$\varphi:X\to Y$ with comorphism $\varphi^*:B\to A$ satisfies
$\varphi^*\mathfrak m_{\varphi(x)}\subseteq\mathfrak m_x$, hence induces
$\mathfrak m_{\varphi(x)}/\mathfrak m_{\varphi(x)}^2\to
\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2$; the dual linear map
$d\varphi_x:T_xX\to T_{\varphi(x)}Y$ is the *differential* of $\varphi$
at $x$. In the dual-number description it is composition with
$\varphi^*$; in particular $d(\psi\circ\varphi)_x=d\psi_{\varphi(x)}\circ
d\varphi_x$.

*Lie algebra of a matrix group.* Let $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be
a closed subgroup scheme of finite type (see the last paragraph), for
example a smooth matrix group. For a commutative $k$-algebra $R$, the
$R$-points $G(R)$ are the matrices in $\operatorname{GL}(V\otimes_kR)$
satisfying the defining equations of $G$ over $R$. For any group scheme
$G$ over $k$ with unit section $e$, the *Lie algebra* is
$\operatorname{Lie}(G)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(e^*\Omega^1_{G/k},k)=T_1G$,
the tangent space at $1$, which is also the *tangent group*
$\ker\big(G(k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2)\to G(k)\big)$ of dual-number points
reducing to $1$; its bracket is the mixed term of the commutator of two
such points over $k[\varepsilon,\delta]/(\varepsilon^2,\delta^2)$. For
$G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$, by the dual-number description, and
identifying $T_1\operatorname{GL}(V)=\operatorname{End}(V)$ through
$X\mapsto1+\varepsilon X$,

$$
\operatorname{Lie}(G)=\{X\in\operatorname{End}(V):
1+\varepsilon X\in G(k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2)\},
$$

a Lie algebra in the sense of [def-wf-lie-algebra] under the bracket
$[X,Y]=XY-YX$ of $\operatorname{End}(V)$; for $G=\operatorname{GL}_n$ this
identifies $\operatorname{Lie}(\operatorname{GL}_n)$ with
$\mathfrak{gl}_n(k)$ as Lie algebras.

*Rational actions.* A *rational representation* of a group scheme $G$
over $k$ on $M=k^m$ is a homomorphism of group schemes
$r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(M)=\operatorname{GL}_m$ over $k$; for a matrix
group $G$ it is a regular homomorphism, i.e. an algebraic-group
module in the sense of [def-wf-algebraic-representations]. Its
differential at $1$ is the linear map
$dr:\operatorname{Lie}(G)\to\operatorname{End}(M)$ characterized by
$r(1+\varepsilon X)=1+\varepsilon\,dr(X)$ over
$k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$ (in general, the differential of $r$ read in
$\mathfrak{gl}_m$ through $\operatorname{Lie}(\operatorname{GL}_m)=\mathfrak{gl}_m$);
it is a Lie representation of
$\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ on $M$ in the sense of [def-wf-lie-algebra],
i.e. $dr([X,Y])=dr(X)dr(Y)-dr(Y)dr(X)$. The *adjoint action*
is $\operatorname{Ad}(g)X=gXg^{-1}$ for $g\in G(k)$, preserving
$\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ because conjugation by $g$ preserves $G$; its
differential is $\operatorname{ad}(Y)X=[Y,X]$.

*Matrix group schemes and smoothness.* A *finite-type matrix group
scheme* is a closed subscheme $\mathcal G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$
cut out by a finitely generated, possibly nonradical, ideal, such that
the regular multiplication and inversion of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$
restrict to it; its coordinate algebra need not a priori be reduced,
and its tangent spaces and Lie algebra are defined by the same formulas
as above, directly from the defining equations. For a closed point $x$
of a finite-type affine $k$-scheme $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$, the *local
ring* is $\mathcal O_{X,x}=A_{\mathfrak m_x}$; it is *regular* if
$\dim_kT_xX=\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}$ (Krull dimension; the inequality
$\ge$ always holds), and $X$ is *smooth over $k$ at $x$* when
$\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is regular ($k$ being algebraically closed of
characteristic zero, hence perfect). A *smooth matrix group* is a
matrix group smooth at every closed point.

proof.text:
*The dual-number description of $T_xX$.* A $k$-algebra map
$A\to k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$ reducing to evaluation at $x$ has the
form $f\mapsto f(x)+\varepsilon\,v(f)$ with $v$ a $k$-derivation at $x$.
The Leibniz rule forces $v(\mathfrak m_x^2)=0$ and $v(1)=0$, so
$v|_{\mathfrak m_x}$ is a linear form killing $\mathfrak m_x^2$; conversely
every such form extends uniquely to a derivation at $x$ via
$A=k\oplus\mathfrak m_x$. The chain rule follows because the dual-number
description of the differential is composition with comorphisms.

*The Lie algebra and the adjoint action.* That
$\operatorname{Lie}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{End}(V)$ is closed under the
bracket, and that $dr$ preserves brackets, is standard (Milne,
*Algebraic Groups* (2017), Chapter 10). For the adjoint action, over
$k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$ one has
$(1+\varepsilon Y)X(1+\varepsilon Y)^{-1}=X+\varepsilon(YX-XY)$, so the
differential of $\operatorname{Ad}$ is $\operatorname{ad}(Y)X=[Y,X]$.
